set.body:
VERIFIED, and filed as a consistency question rather than a defect, because the behaviour is ordinary R and many users will want it.

  named  c(a=1, b=-1, c=0)    signed =  0.22500
  posn   c(1, -1, 0)          signed =  0.22500     same thing
  posn   c(0, 1, -1)          signed = -0.25000     a DIFFERENT contrast, no warning
  named  c(c=0, b=-1, a=1)    signed =  0.22500     names win over order, correctly

So contrast() honours names when present and falls back to POSITION when absent. A user who supplies unnamed weights in the wrong order silently computes a different contrast and gets a plausible number back.

THE VALIDATION ASYMMETRY IS THE INTERESTING PART. Named weights are strictly checked - a wrong name produces 'Named contrast weights must identify every effect exactly once', and a wrong length produces 'A contrast must contain one finite numeric weight per effect'. Unnamed weights receive no identity check at all, because there is nothing to check. So the MORE careful user, who names their weights, is protected, and the LESS careful user, who does not, is not. The protection is opt-in and the failure is silent.

WHY IT IS WORTH RECORDING DESPITE BEING STANDARD PRACTICE. This package's stated position, repeated across the README and both vignettes, is that a matching name and dimension cannot substitute for a declared identity - and it enforces that seriously elsewhere, refusing relations whose domains merely happen to agree in size and forcing partition independence to be asserted rather than assumed. Accepting a bare numeric vector as a contrast is exactly the inference the rest of the package refuses: it reads identity off position.

I am NOT proposing that positional weights be removed. c(1,-1,0) is idiomatic R, it is what people will type, and breaking it would cost more than it saves.

WHAT I WOULD PROPOSE, weakest first:
  1. document that unnamed weights are positional and are matched against the effect order,
     and say where that order comes from - the effect_space coordinates
  2. have print() on the contrast view report the resolved weights WITH names attached, so a
     mis-ordered positional contrast becomes visible in the output rather than silent
  3. optionally, a strict mode in which unnamed weights are refused

Option 2 is the cheapest and probably sufficient: the user sees which effect got which weight in the thing they were going to read anyway. It also serves bd-01KZYAPHG7H569TNBPE4XV8WXN, which is about outputs not saying what their rows and columns mean.
set.title: Positional contrast weights are accepted, contradicting the package's own stance on inferred identity
